prompt: A PR passes all CI checks and the feature works when manually tested. According to this lesson, what does that tell you?
choices: The review is effectively done; CI passing is the main signal that matters
Only that the code compiles and the happy path works — review still needs to check correctness on edge cases, readability, test quality, security patterns, and architectural fit
That the tests are sufficient, so review should focus only on style
That security review is unnecessary since a working build implies no injection risks

prompt: Which review comment is written in the actionable style described in this lesson?
choices: "This function is messy, please clean it up."
"Not a fan of this approach."

"Line 14 concatenates `filename` directly into the shell command via f-string — if `filename` ever comes from user input, this is command injection. Use `subprocess.run([cmd, filename])` instead of a shell string."
"Security issue here, fix before merging."

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend reviewing against a checklist instead of reading a diff and commenting on whatever stands out?
choices: Checklists are required by most CI systems
Vibe review is slower because reviewers overthink every line

A checklist forces you to check categories that don't naturally catch your eye, so the same class of bug (missing null check, unhandled error path, undiscussed new dependency) doesn't keep slipping through
Checklists eliminate the need for a human reviewer entirely

prompt: You're reviewing this code: `db.query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = {user_id}")` where `user_id` comes from a URL path parameter. What's the correct actionable feedback?
choices: No comment needed — f-strings are just a Python formatting convenience
"This is bad practice."
Point out that `user_id` is interpolated directly into the SQL string, which is a SQL injection risk since it comes from user-controlled input, and suggest a parameterized query instead
Suggest renaming `user_id` to something clearer

prompt: A loop in a PR issues one database query per item in a list that can have hundreds of entries. What pattern is this, and what's the fix direction?
choices: This is expected behavior; databases are optimized for many small queries
N+1 queries — fix by fetching all the needed rows in a single batched query (e.g. an IN/ANY clause) instead of one query per item
A race condition — fix by adding a lock around the loop
A memory leak — fix by adding garbage collection calls inside the loop

prompt: According to this lesson, why is vague feedback like "needs more tests" actually the less kind option, not just the less useful one?
choices: Because it's technically incorrect — the code never needs more tests
Because it dumps the diagnostic work of figuring out what's actually missing back onto the author while still implying their work was inadequate, instead of naming the specific gap
Because vague comments take longer to write than specific ones
Because reviewers should never ask for more tests under any circumstance

prompt: A reviewer notices a PR adds a brand-new HTTP client library to make one API call, when the codebase already has a shared HTTP client used everywhere else. Which review category does this fall under, and what should the reviewer do?
choices: Readability — suggest renaming the new client for clarity
Architectural fit — flag that this duplicates an existing solution and ask the author to use the shared client instead, or explain why it doesn't fit here
Test coverage — the main issue is that the new library isn't tested
This isn't something code review should catch; it's a build/tooling concern

prompt: A reviewer leaves a comment reading "Nit: could shorten this with a list comprehension, up to you" versus "Blocking: this will throw an unhandled exception on a missing user." What is the purpose of explicitly labeling comments this way?
choices: It has no real purpose beyond formatting preference
It lets the author distinguish must-fix issues from optional suggestions, so they don't have to either fight every comment or ignore all of them
It's required by most code review tools to sort comments automatically
It signals which comments the reviewer personally wrote versus ones generated by a linter
